content: The Tine test is a diagnostic tool used to assist in identifying tuberculosis (TB). It is a type of tuberculin skin test that employs a small device, often referred to as a button, which contains four to six short needles coated with TB antigens, specifically tuberculin. These needles are pressed into the skin, typically on the inner side of the forearm, to introduce the antigens into the dermis. The test result is interpreted by measuring the size of the largest papule (a raised, red bump) that forms at the site of application. A negative result is indicated by the absence of any papules. However, due to the inability to precisely control the amount of tuberculin delivered by the Tine test, a positive result must be confirmed using the more standardized Mantoux test. The Tine test is considered less reliable than the Mantoux test and is not as widely utilized. It is not recommended for use by the American Thoracic Society or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The Tine test, along with other similar multiple-puncture tuberculin skin tests such as the Aplite test, is generally regarded as an inferior diagnostic method for TB.
